name: Vera Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at a seafood restaurant on the harbour, mostly on the fish section: cleaning, filleting and cooking whatever the boats bring in. We do about 150 covers a night in summer and half that in winter. I use AI every day, for working out fish prices, writing the specials board and checking allergy information.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the mornings on the quay, when the boats come in and I pick the fish with the owner. What wears me out is winter, because the hours drop and so does the pay. My husband Erik builds boats at the yard down the road, so our money moves with the seasons too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's all, which is what I already tell people. Some of the older cooks think I cheat by using it. I might post about it in the cooks' group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries in that world are the winter hours and getting my own place, not AI. My mum wants to retire from her bakery in the village in three years, and I'd like to take it over and add lunches. That's the big decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at the harbour and keep using AI to cost a lunch menu for the bakery. Erik and I would put his winter overtime from the yard toward buying Mum's ovens off her. And we'd try for a baby in about two years, same as we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy in my head, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some savings, about four months' worth, plus a small loan, and Mum would let us pay her over time. I've already had the AI draft a business plan, which she read with her glasses on the end of her nose. My mum has baked bread by hand for 30 years, and now she lets my AI app check her sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the winter hours still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, every year. The restaurant drops to four days a week in January. That's part of why I want my own place, so I set the hours.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd shrug off older cooks who think using it is **cheating**.
think: Privately my real worries are **winter hours** and getting my own place.
Taking over my mum's **village bakery** in three years is the big decision.
do: Use AI to **cost a lunch menu** for the bakery.
Put my husband's **winter overtime** towards buying the bakery ovens.
Try for a **baby** in about two years, as planned.
feel: **Calm**, though her head is busy with plans.
S0.quote: My mum has baked bread by hand for 30 years, and now she lets my AI app check her sums.
fieldNote: For her, the plateau is simply **business as usual** with a plan already in motion.
She uses AI daily yet frames it within a **family business** passed down by her mother.
**Seasonal pay** for both her and her husband is the main money strain.

steps.text: Keep cooking fish at the harbour restaurant through the season
Put her husband's winter overtime towards buying the bakery ovens
Try for a baby in about two years as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the computers do the paperwork and let cooks cook. That's what I'd tell anyone moaning at work. I'd mean it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it suits me. The bakery's ordering, bookings and accounts would be cheap to run with AI, which makes taking over Mum's place easier. The robots are slow on hands-on work, so the baking and cooking stay mine for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the bakery on a year early and set it up from day one with AI for orders, stock and the books. I'd stay part-time at the harbour for the steady wage during the first year. I'd also take a weekend course in food business accounts, so I can check what the software tells me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Quite a lot of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman who does the bookings at the harbour, and probably the accountant in the village who does Mum's books. I feel for them, but nobody owes anybody a job. I'd rather pay software to do the bakery's books and pay a local teenager to serve the coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your plans for a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If anything, my own bakery makes it easier. Mum did it with me in a basket behind the counter, and that's how families used to work.

I'd tell anyone moaning at work that this is **good news**.
think: Privately, cheap AI for orders and accounts makes **taking over** the bakery easier.
Slow robots mean the **baking and cooking** stay mine for years.
do: Take over the **bakery** a year earlier than planned.
Run orders, stock and the books on **AI** from day one.
Stay **part-time** at the harbour restaurant for the first year.
S1.quote: I'd rather pay software to do the bakery's books and pay a local teenager to serve the coffee.
fieldNote: She reads Steady Disruption as an **advantage** for a small owner.
Her **free-market** view shows when she says nobody owes anybody a job.
She sees running a family business as **compatible with motherhood**, like her own mother did.

steps.text: Take over her mum's bakery a year earlier than planned
Run the bakery's orders, stock and books on AI from day one
Stay part-time at the harbour restaurant for a steady wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to own something. People who own the business will do better than people who work for one. I'd say that kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is fast even for me. The business side is easy with AGI, but by 2031 robots can bake and cook too, and then why would anyone pay my prices? I'd be 32, maybe with a toddler, and the bakery would be competing with a robot at the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the bakery right away, while Mum can still show me everything. I'd build it around being the local place where you know the baker, with Sunday cakes for church and orders for weddings and funerals. And I'd buy one of the first robot dough machines once they're out, so I'm the one using them, not the one beaten by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and fired up at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the baby still come in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about it, but yes. Erik's boatyard would probably get robots later than most, because every boat is different. I won't put off having a baby because of a computer. My grandmother had four children in harder times than these.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the robots that might beat you. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I think. If a machine can knead the dough at four in the morning, I get to sleep. People still want to buy from a person, but the person doesn't need to do every step.

I'd tell people that **owners** will do better than employees.
think: Privately, robots that can bake by **2031** could undercut my prices.
I'd be **32**, maybe with a toddler, competing with a supermarket robot.
do: Take over the **bakery** straight away while my mum can still teach me.
Build trade around **church cakes**, weddings and funerals.
Buy one of the first **robot dough machines** when they appear.
S2.quote: I won't put off having a baby because of a computer. My grandmother had four children in harder times than these.
fieldNote: Even an early adopter finds **two years** fast when the robots reach her craft.
Her answer is to **own and automate** before competitors do.
She refuses to let technology **delay a baby**, citing her grandmother's generation.

steps.text: Take over her mum's bakery straight away while her mum can teach
Build bakery trade around church cakes, weddings and funerals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say get ready and own something. Same as before, just with less panic. I'd tell the young cooks to learn the business side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, five years is about right for me. I'd have the bakery running for two years before AGI, and five or six years before robots can bake, around 2034. By then the regulars know us, and that's worth something a robot can't buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the bakery on the original timeline, in three years. Until then I'd keep cooking at the harbour and use AI to build the bakery's ordering system and website. We'd have the baby on the planned timeline too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A bit of an itch to get moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the first day AGI arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hand it the boring jobs: the tax forms, the supplier emails, the rota. Then I'd go back to the ovens. When the computers can do the paperwork, I'll finally have time to bake the way my mum taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the bakery failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Myself, honestly. Nobody makes you open a business. If it goes, it goes, and I'd go back to cooking for someone else while there's still cooking to do.

say: I'd say **get ready** and own something, just with less panic.
I'd tell young cooks to learn the **business side** now.
think: Privately, five years gives the bakery **regulars** before robots can bake around 2034.
Local **loyalty** is something a robot can't buy.
do: Take over the bakery on the original **three-year** timeline.
Use AI to build the bakery's **ordering system** and website.
Keep cooking at the **harbour** until the bakery opens.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with an itch to get moving.
S3.quote: When the computers can do the paperwork, I'll finally have time to bake the way my mum taught me.
fieldNote: She'd hand AGI the **paperwork** and keep the craft for herself.
She takes full **personal responsibility** for the business, blaming no one else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say lucky us. Plenty of time to build something. And I'd tell anyone who complains that they've been warned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me calm. The bakery would be about seven years old by the time AGI arrives in 2036, and robots would come around 2039, when I'm 40. By then I'd want two shops and a reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over Mum's bakery on schedule and open a second small shop in the next town by year six. I'd use every AI tool going on the business side and bring in robot help for the night baking when it's proven safe and cheap. And we'd have our children and not think twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik, a little. The boatyard's owner is old and doesn't like computers. If the yard doesn't change, it might close before the robots even get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Erik about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should come and do the deliveries and fix the ovens for us. He'd laugh. My husband Erik can build a whole boat by hand, so he can manage a delivery van and a broken oven.

say: I'd say ten years means **lucky us**, with plenty of time to build.
think: Privately, ten years makes me **calm**, with robots arriving when I'm 40.
By then I'd want **two shops** and a solid reputation.
do: Open a **second shop** in the next town by year six.
Bring in **robot help** for night baking once it's proven.
S4.quote: My husband Erik can build a whole boat by hand, so he can manage a delivery van and a broken oven.
fieldNote: With a decade she plans **growth**, not defence.
Her only worry is her husband's **boatyard**, run by an owner who avoids computers.
She'd bring her husband **into the bakery** if his yard closed.

steps.text: Open a second small bakery in the next town by year six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the robots would arrive while I'm still paying off the bakery, maybe with a toddler. What would help is small-business loans that are cheap, simple and quick, and rules that let a small bakery buy a robot oven the same year a supermarket does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my faith, and it matters to me. I trust God with the big picture and AI with the tax forms, and I keep my hands for the bread.

headlineQuote: I trust God with the big picture and AI with the tax forms, and I keep my hands for the bread.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old fish cook** at a harbour seafood restaurant who uses AI every day.
She's married to Erik, a **boatbuilder**, and they plan a baby in about two years.
Her plan is to take over her mum's **village bakery** and run its business side with AI.
She sees Steady Disruption as an **advantage**, and answers fast AGI by owning and automating early.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her nervous, because robots could arrive before the bakery is paid off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots arriving while she still owes on the bakery and may have a toddler.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, quick small-business loans** for owners like her.
Rules that let a **small bakery** buy robot ovens as early as a supermarket.
